### 3. Implication dans la vernalisation

Une multitude d’études a montré l’implication des mécanismes épigénétiques dans la vernalisation, [SOURCE: Page_256]

terme décrivant le processus qui promeut la floraison après une période de froid prolongée. La [SOURCE: Page_256]

vernalisation et son gène central (FLC) sont ainsi devenus l’exemple clé de mécanisme épigénétique en [SOURCE: Page_256]

lien avec le développement, la réponse à un changement environnemental et la mémoire épigénétique [SOURCE: Page_256]

(Song et al., 2012a ; Whittaker & Dean, 2017). Une première étude est celle de Burn et al. (1993) qui a [SOURCE: Page_256]

traité une plante, Thlaspi arvense, avec une drogue hypométhylante, la 5-azacytidine. Ce composé est [SOURCE: Page_256]

un analogue à la cytidine et agit comme un inhibiteur des méthyltransférases, engendrant une [SOURCE: Page_256]

hypométhylation du génome. Les plants de Thlaspi arvense ainsi traités ont fleuri précocement sans [SOURCE: Page_256]

vernalisation. De même, le froid induit une hypométhylation du génome et l’étude de mutants pour le [SOURCE: Page_256]

gène codant l’ADN méthyltransférase MET$_1$ présente également une floraison précoce ce qui suggère [SOURCE: Page_256]

que la déméthylation permet la floraison (Ronemus et al., 1996). Cependant, le locus central de la [SOURCE: Page_256]

vernalisation (FLC) n’est la cible d’aucune variation de méthylation lors de la vernalisation, ce qui a [SOURCE: Page_256]

réorienté les travaux de recherche vers les modifications d’histones (Finnegan et al., 2005). [SOURCE: Page_256]

Durant le processus de vernalisation, le froid induit l’expression du gène VIN$_3$ qui va engendrer [SOURCE: Page_256]

la désacétylation des histones H$_3$ du gène FLC (Figure II.5). Lorsque la période de froid persiste, [SOURCE: Page_256]

l’expression du gène VIN$_3$ va engendrer le recrutement de la protéine VRN$_2$. Cette dernière va méthyler [SOURCE: Page_256]

les histones H$_3$ et inhiber le gène FLC qui réprime de manière constitutive la floraison. La durée de la [SOURCE: Page_256]

période de froid est mise en mémoire de manière quantitative, jusqu’à l’embryogenèse où la réactivation [SOURCE: Page_256]

du gène FLC remet à zéro la vernalisation(Baulcombe and Dean, 2014; Whittaker and Dean, 2017; [SOURCE: Page_256]

Itabashi et al., 2018) [SOURCE: Page_256]

le froid ce qui contribue à la répression du gène FLC (Tian et al., 2019). Ces exemples montrent le lien [SOURCE: Page_258]

Le processus de vernalisation a également été étudié chez d’autres espèces végétales d’intérêt [SOURCE: Page_258]

sucrière, il a été montré que plusieurs loci importants de la floraison étaient affectés directement par la [SOURCE: Page_258]

4. Épigénétique, plasticité phénotypique et adaptation [SOURCE: Page_260]

4.1.Epigénome et plasticité [SOURCE: Page_260]

La plasticité phénotypique est la capacité pour un génotype d’exprimer différents phénotypes en [SOURCE: Page_260]

fonction de l’environnement. Cette dernière peut être adaptative lorsque l’environnement change la [SOURCE: Page_260]

distribution des phénotypes vers l’optimum local (Ghalambor et al., 2007). Compte tenu de la relation [SOURCE: Page_260]

existant entre épigénétique et plasticité phénotypique, certaines études se sont intéressées au lien entre [SOURCE: Page_260]

ces deux concepts (Baulcombe and Dean, 2014; Kooke et al., 2015). D’autres études ont révélé que des [SOURCE: Page_260]

environnements stressants induisent chez les plantes des changements épigénétiques pouvant conduire [SOURCE: Page_260]

à des changements phénotypiques et des réponses adaptatives (Cubas et al., 1999; Kooke et al., 2015; [SOURCE: Page_260]

Meyer, 2015 ; Conde et al., 2017 ; Seymour and Becker, 2017 ; He and Li, 2018 ; Lafon-Placette et al., [SOURCE: Page_260]

2018). [SOURCE: Page_260]

Les modifications épigénétiques, engendrées par l’environnement, permettent à un organisme [SOURCE: Page_260]

une meilleure survie et d’exprimer une plus grande plasticité. Ainsi, Zhang et al. (2013) travaillent sur [SOURCE: Page_260]

des lignées epiRILS chez Arabidopsis thaliana, lignées qui ne diffèrent que par les zones méthylées de [SOURCE: Page_260]

l’ADN, et étudient leurs réponses face à la sécheresse et à l’augmentation des nutriments. Leurs résultats [SOURCE: Page_260]

montrent des variations parmi les epiRILs sur des traits phénotypiques importants tels que le ratio de la [SOURCE: Page_260]

biomasse sèche entre racine et tige, ce qui suggère un lien étroit entre plasticité phénotypique et [SOURCE: Page_260]

mécanismes épigénétiques. Kooke et al. (2015) ont étudié 99 epiRIL d’A. thaliana et leurs parents Col- [SOURCE: Page_260]

0 et ddm^1-2 sous stress salin. Ils ont montré que l’hypométhylation de l’ADN engendre des plantes plus [SOURCE: Page_260]

sensibles au stress appliqué. En outre, ils ont identifié des QTLs (locus de caractères quantitatifs) [SOURCE: Page_260]

associés aux traits morphologiques (ramification et surface foliaire) et des QTLs associés à la plasticité [SOURCE: Page_260]

phénotypique. Ces deux types de QTL colocalisent ce qui suggère l’existence d’un effet pléiotropique [SOURCE: Page_260]

entre eux. Les processus dans lesquels sont impliqués les marques épigénétiques, et leur caractère [SOURCE: Page_260]

réversible, rapide et parfois transgénérationnel, ont conduit les chercheurs à se poser la question de [SOURCE: Page_260]

l’implication de l’épigénome comme source d’adaptation rapide (Henderson & Jacobsen, 2007 ; [SOURCE: Page_260]

Kawakatsu et al., 2016 ; Weinhold, 2018 ; Thiebaut et al., 2019). [SOURCE: Page_260]

226 [SOURCE: Page_261]

Figure II-7 : Les différents niveaux de l’adaptation selon Yona et al. (2015). [SOURCE: Page_261]

Deux temporalités caractérisent les différents niveaux d’adaptation : le temps nécessaire à l’acquisition de l’adaptation (axe de gauche) et le temps pour que cette adaptation soit maintenue en l’absence des conditions requises pour l’adaptation. Les adaptations physiologiques consistent en des changements de l’homéostasie biochimique, et donc leur durée dépend de la durée de vie des biomolécules qui sous- tendent l’adaptation, comme les ARNm, les protéines, etc. Les modifications épigénétiques se produisent généralement dans la même génération que l’expérience du déclencheur, mais leur durée dépend du type de mécanisme épigénétique, p. ex., méthylation de l’ADN, modification de la chromatine, prions, etc. (revu par Rando et Verstrepen, 2007). Les dédoublements génomiques comprennent les dédoublements segmentaires et l’aneuploïdie résultant d’erreur dans la ségrégation chromosomique au cours du cycle cellulaire, ce qui entraîne des changements bruts dans l’expression génétique de la région dupliquée. Les mutations génétiques sont des modifications fonctionnelles de la séquence codante ou des régions régulatrices de gènes qui modifient leur fonction ou leur expression. [SOURCE: Page_261]

227 [SOURCE: Page_262]

4.2.Epigénome et adaptation [SOURCE: Page_262]

L’épigénétique intervient donc dans des processus de réponse à l’environnement et de mémoire des [SOURCE: Page_262]

stress notamment à travers la plasticité phénotypique. La question du rôle de l’épigénétique dans [SOURCE: Page_262]

l’adaptation se pose. En effet, l’adaptation reflète les changements morphologiques, physiologiques [SOURCE: Page_262]

d’un individu qui permettent à une population ou espèce de persister dans le temps à travers des [SOURCE: Page_262]

mécanismes génétiques et non génétiques (Yona et al., 2015). Ces auteurs distinguent ainsi deux [SOURCE: Page_262]

temporalités dans l’adaptation. La première correspond au temps nécessaire à l’acquisition qui est rapide [SOURCE: Page_262]

pour des changements physiologiques impliquant des protéines et des ARNm et plus long concernant [SOURCE: Page_262]

les mutations génétiques. La seconde temporalité est le temps pour que l’adaptation soit maintenue. [SOURCE: Page_262]

Ainsi les changements physiologiques ne perdurent que lorsque la contrainte est là, alors que les [SOURCE: Page_262]

mutations génétiques sont aisément transmises à la descendance pour peu que les cellules germinales [SOURCE: Page_262]

soient touchées et perdurent dans le temps (Figure II.7). Les mécanismes épigénétiques sont difficiles à [SOURCE: Page_262]

placer sur ces deux temporalités. En effet, l’héritabilité des marques épigénétiques par mitose et/ou par [SOURCE: Page_262]

méiose est centrale pour déterminer l’importance que peut avoir l’épigénétique dans l’adaptation. Il reste [SOURCE: Page_262]

maintenant à savoir si des modifications épigénétiques induites par l’environnement peuvent se [SOURCE: Page_262]

transmettre sur plusieurs générations. [SOURCE: Page_262]

Lämke & Bäurle, (2017) font la distinction entre les modifications inter et transgénérationnelles. [SOURCE: Page_262]

Dans le premier cas, l’environnement du parent peut affecter directement les cellules germinales de la [SOURCE: Page_262]

progéniture. Dans le second cas, un effet transgénérationnel est défini si, à partir d’une lignée germinale [SOURCE: Page_262]

de la génération F$_2$ qui n’a pas été exposée à la contrainte environnementale étudiée, on retrouve des [SOURCE: Page_262]

effets à la troisième génération (F$_3$) et éventuellement aux générations futures. Ainsi, Wibowo et al. [SOURCE: Page_262]

(2016) ont étudié, chez A. thaliana, l’effet du stress osmotique sur plusieurs générations. Ils montrent [SOURCE: Page_262]

qu’il y a transmission d’une mémoire du stress par la lignée germinale femelle sur une génération. En [SOURCE: Page_262]

effet, via l’utilisation de mutant pour le gène DEMETER (DME) ils montrent que l’activité d’une ADN [SOURCE: Page_262]

glycosylase dans la lignée germinale mâle engendre une reprogrammation épigénétique. Cette [SOURCE: Page_262]

transmission est perdue dès lors que le stress n’est pas maintenu. C’est donc un cas de mémoire [SOURCE: Page_262]

intergénérationnelle, celle-ci étant ici liée à la méthylation de l’ADN. Les études réalisées par Reinders [SOURCE: Page_262]

228 [SOURCE: Page_263]

Tableau II-2. Les effets du stress héritable sur la stabilité du génome et de l’épigénome des plantes. (Hauser et al., 2011) [SOURCE: Page_263]

229 [SOURCE: Page_264]

et al (2009) et Johannes et al (2009), avec des lignées epiRILS d’un croisement impliquant un mutant [SOURCE: Page_264]

ddm^1 ou met^1 avec le type sauvage chez A. thaliana, montrent une stabilité des marques de méthylation [SOURCE: Page_264]

de l’ADN durant près de 8 générations. En outre, ces différences de profil de méthylation entre lignées [SOURCE: Page_264]

étaient corrélées à des traits comme la floraison ou la résistance à des pathogènes. Le gène FWA [SOURCE: Page_264]

(FLOWERING WAGENINGEN) est méthylé chez le type sauvage, mais déméthylé chez met^1-3 [SOURCE: Page_264]

provoquant un retard dans la floraison chez le mutant. Hauser et al. (2011) listent ainsi dans un tableau [SOURCE: Page_264]

les différentes études montrant des effets transgénérationnels liés au stress (Table II.2). Parmi celles-ci, [SOURCE: Page_264]

on constate que les descendants, dont le parent a subi un stress, sont plus tolérants à ce stress et présentent [SOURCE: Page_264]

des modifications de profil de méthylation. On peut également citer Alsdurf et al. (2016) qui ont étudié [SOURCE: Page_264]

la plante pérenne Boechera strictaune. Ils ont montré une meilleure tolérance à la sécheresse chez des [SOURCE: Page_264]

descendants issus de plantes ayant subi le stress et cela en lien avec la méthylation. Néanmoins, tout [SOURCE: Page_264]

comme chez Wibowo et al. (2016), les modifications épigénétiques s’estompent après quelques [SOURCE: Page_264]

générations. Parfois ces modifications perdurent durant près de 9 générations comme c’est le cas dans [SOURCE: Page_264]

l’étude de Akimoto et al. (2007). Dans cette étude, des graines de riz ont été traitées avec un agent [SOURCE: Page_264]

chimique hypométhylant, la 5 azadeoxycytidine, et après 9 générations, des gènes restent hypométhylés [SOURCE: Page_264]

et activés, ces derniers conférant une résistance à une souche de Xanthomonas. La mémoire des stress, [SOURCE: Page_264]

à travers des mécanismes épigénétiques, permet alors un meilleur ajustement de l’organisme aux [SOURCE: Page_264]

contraintes biotiques et abiotiques sur des temps plus ou moins longs. En outre, chez A. thaliana, la [SOURCE: Page_264]

fréquence des épimutations a été estimée à 4,46×10−4 Single Methylation Polymorphisms (SMP) par [SOURCE: Page_264]

site CG pour une génération, contre une fréquence de 7× 10−9 mutation par site CG et par génération [SOURCE: Page_264]

(Ossowski et al., 2010 ; van der Graaf et al., 2015). De plus en plus de preuves s’accumulent et montrent [SOURCE: Page_264]

que les marques épigénétiques peuvent être transmises à travers les générations. Si la capacité des [SOURCE: Page_264]

modifications épigénétiques à se transmettre à la descendance est importante pour jouer un rôle dans [SOURCE: Page_264]

l’adaptation, leur caractère réversible permet un ajustement aux conditions environnementales. [SOURCE: Page_264]

Pour évaluer la contribution de l’épigénétique à l’adaptation, Schmid et al. (2018) ont étudié [SOURCE: Page_264]

chez A. thaliana, 17 RILs et leurs deux parents, après 5 générations mimant la sélection. Suite à la [SOURCE: Page_264]

sélection, deux génotypes dominaient la population. Ils ont ensuite comparé les traits phénotypiques et [SOURCE: Page_264]

230 [SOURCE: Page_265]

a. une représentation schématique de la conception expérimentale. La population originale se composait de 19 génotypes également représentés mis en culture dans un environnement sélectif durant 5 générations. Deux génotypes (Rils CVL39 et CVL125) ont dominé les populations sélectionnées et ont été utilisés dans cette étude. Les descendants provenant de la population originale (D$_0$) et de populations sélectionnées (provenant de trois expériences indépendantes, c’est-à-dire des paysages D$_1$, D$_5$, etD$_6$) ont été cultivés pendant trois générations dans un environnement non sélectif (conditions contrôlées et emplacements aléatoires des plantes). Les phénotypes ont été mesurés dans la deuxième et la troisième génération. Méthylome et transcriptome ont été profilés dans la deuxième génération. Les génomes ont été séquencés à la troisième génération. b Comparaison des caractères phénotypiques de la descendance des populations ancestrales (D$_0$) et sélectionnées (D$_1$/D$_5$/D$_6$). Dans la deuxième et troisième génération, le temps de floraison a été considérablement retardé et le nombre d’inflorescences secondaires a été considérablement augmenté dans le sélectionné par rapport à la population ancestrale (données supplémentaires 1). Pour montrer les deux générations à la fois, les chiffres indiqués sont des différences par rapport aux moyennes pour toutes les populations d’ungénotype au sein d’une génération donnée. c La distance moyenne de paires (MPD) dans les modèles de méthylation de l’ADN entre les individus d’une population donnéereflète la diversité épigénétique au sein de la population. Dans la deuxième génération, la diversité épigénétique était constamment plus élevée dans les populations ancestrales(D$_0$) par rapport aux populations sélectionnées (D$_1$/D$_5$/D$_6$) [SOURCE: Page_265]

### 5.1. Présentation synthétique de la publication Marin/Genitoni et al. 2019

Une espèce invasive a dû, par définition, coloniser de nouveaux milieux et s’adapter rapidement à de [SOURCE: Page_268]

nouvelles contraintes environnementales. Les scientifiques ont longtemps vu le succès des invasions [SOURCE: Page_268]

biologiques comme un paradoxe. L’effet de goulet d’étranglement subi par la population devrait [SOURCE: Page_268]

engendrer une réduction de son potentiel adaptatif. Parmi les hypothèses pouvant expliquer l’invalidité [SOURCE: Page_268]

de ce paradoxe, on retrouve notamment les mécanismes épigénétiques (Estoup et al., 2016 ; Stapley et [SOURCE: Page_268]

al., 2017). Comme nous l’avons vu précédemment, l’épigénétique est un moyen pour un organisme [SOURCE: Page_268]

d’exprimer une plus grande plasticité. Cette dernière fait partie intégrante des nombreux déterminants [SOURCE: Page_268]

qui interviennent dans la réussite d’une invasion biologique. On retrouve l’idée communément admise [SOURCE: Page_268]

que ces espèces invasives possèdent une plasticité phénotypique plus importante que les espèces dites [SOURCE: Page_268]

natives (Davidson et al., 2011 ; Ghalambor et al., 2007). [SOURCE: Page_268]

Nous avons cherché à comprendre les mécanismes régissant les invasions biologiques et leur [SOURCE: Page_268]

adaptation rapide à de nouveaux milieux. Deux mécanismes ont été étudiés : les éléments transposables [SOURCE: Page_268]

et les modifications épigénétiques. En effet, les liens entre invasions biologiques, plasticité [SOURCE: Page_268]

phénotypique, épigénétique et éléments transposables n’étaient pas clairement synthétisés dans la [SOURCE: Page_268]

littérature existante et nous avons valorisé ce travail bibliographique sous la forme d’un article de [SOURCE: Page_268]

synthèse intitulé “Biological invasion: The influence of the hidden side of the (epi)genome” publié dans [SOURCE: Page_268]

Functional Ecology. [SOURCE: Page_268]

Dans le sillage de Prentis et al. (2008), Rey et al (2016) et Vogt, (2017), nous posons l’hypothèse [SOURCE: Page_268]

d’un rôle primordial des éléments transposables et des mécanismes épigénétiques dans le succès des [SOURCE: Page_268]

invasions biologiques. Ces processus sont encore trop peu étudiés chez les espèces invasives. Dans un [SOURCE: Page_268]

premier temps, nous nous sommes intéressés aux éléments transposables. Nous avons repositionné leur [SOURCE: Page_268]

rôle et comment ils sont régulés dans le génome. Puis, nous nous sommes attardés sur la manière dont [SOURCE: Page_268]

ils interagissent avec l’environnement et notamment les stress abiotiques et biotiques. Et enfin, nous [SOURCE: Page_268]

234 [SOURCE: Page_269]

235 [SOURCE: Page_270]

avons regardé leur intégration dans le contexte des invasions biologiques. Dans un second temps, nous [SOURCE: Page_270]

avons fait l’état de l’art des mécanismes épigénétiques comme composante de la réponse aux [SOURCE: Page_270]

changements environnementaux et en particulier chez les espèces invasives. Dans un dernier temps, [SOURCE: Page_270]

nous avons discuté des limites des études et des défis à relever. [SOURCE: Page_270]

## EPIGENETICS IN ECOLOGY AND EVOLUTION – A PRIMER

Biological invasion: The influence of the hidden side of the (epi) genome [SOURCE: Page_272]

Pierre Marin^1* | Julien Genitoni^2,3* | Dominique Barloy^2                                         | Stéphane Maury^3 | Patricia Gibert^1 | Cameron K. Ghalambor^4 | Cristina Vieira^1 [SOURCE: Page_272]

1 Laboratoire de Biométrie et Biologie Evolutive UMR 5558, CNRS, Université Lyon       Abstract 1, Université de Lyon, Villeurbanne, France     1. Understanding the mechanisms underlying biological invasions and rapid adapta- 2 ESE, Ecology and Ecosystem Health, tion to global change remains a fundamental challenge, particularly in small popu- Agrocampus Ouest, INRA, Rennes, France 3 LBLGC EA 1207, INRA, Université lations lacking in genetic variation. Two understudied mechanisms that could d’Orléans, USC 1328, Orléans, France                  facilitate adaptive evolution and adaptive plasticity are the increased genetic vari- 4 Department of Biology and Graduate                   ation due to transposable elements (TEs), and associated or independent modifi- Degree Program in Ecology, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, Colorado                    cation of gene expression through epigenetic changes. 2. Here, we focus on the potential role of these genetic and non-genetic mechanisms Correspondence Cristina Vieira                                       for facilitating invasion success. Because novel or stressful environments are Email: [EMAIL_REDACTED]                  known to induce both epigenetic changes and TE activity, these mechanisms may Funding information                                   play an underappreciated role in generating phenotypic and genetic variation for Institut National de la Recherche                     selection to act on. We review how these mechanisms operate, the evidence for Agronomique; Région Bretagne, France; Fondation Rovaltain; National Science                 how they respond to novel or stressful environments, and how these mechanisms Foundation, Grant/Award Number:                       can contribute to the success of biological invasions by facilitating adaptive evolu- IOS-1457383; Agence Nationale de la Recherche, Grant/Award Number: SWING;                 tion and phenotypic plasticity. Université Claude Bernard Lyon 1                3. Because genetic and phenotypic variations due to TEs and epigenetic changes are Handling Editor: Anthony Herrel                       often well regulated or “hidden” in the native environment, the independent and combined contribution of these mechanisms may only become important when populations colonize novel environments. A focus on the mechanisms that gener- ate and control the expression of this variation in new environments may provide insights into biological invasions that would otherwise not be obvious. 4. Global changes and human activities impact on ecosystems and allow new oppor- tunities for biological invasions. Invasive species succeed by adapting rapidly to new environments. The degree to which rapid responses to environmental change could be mediated by the epigenome—the regulatory system that integrates how environmental and genomic variation jointly shape phenotypic variation—requires greater attention if we want to understand the mechanisms by which populations successfully colonize and adapt to new environments. F I G U R E 1 Process of invasion and its epi/genomics, life mode, environmental and human activity determinants. A species in its native area (white frame) is transported in a new environment (grey frame), often by human activities, voluntary or not. Genetic diversity (blue shape) is recognized as lower in introduced area. Installation of this new population can be facilitated by repeated introductions (propagule pressure). A bottleneck can take place and lead to the disappearance of the introduced species. Organisms who survive can have a different genetic (shape) and epigenetic (colour) diversity than from native area. Population becomes established and continues in time; some species can be naturalized, while others are going to continue their expansion until they become invasive. There is an uncontrolled expansion with a selection of the most performing genetic and epigenetic variants in a given environment. These invasive species can then colonize new environments and cause economic and ecological issues. During this process, a multitude of factors comes into play: Epigenetic and genetic mechanisms can modify gene expression and thus the capacity for local adaptation and phenotypic plasticity. Characteristics of organisms are also important factors to consider for the success of a biological invasion: life cycle, type of multiplication, especially clonal, possibility of hybridization (combined shape) and the capacities of dispersal can favour the installation of the population in a new environment. Environmental factors, biotic and abiotic, represent the sensibility of the ecosystems. Absence of predators and competitors in the introduction area, as noted in enemy release hypothesis (ERH) and its corollary evolution of increased competitive ability (EICA), as well as the presence of empty ecological niche can partially explain the success of an invasion. Besides, global climate change has been identified as a source of opportunity for new invasions. Finally, human activities are a key factor of either success or failure of an invasion. The human being acts at the origin of the process by the action of transport, voluntary or not. On the other hand, he can, with legislation and prevention, decrease or control this mechanism. He can either promote invasions by altering the ecosystems or limit their impact by controlled actions and management [SOURCE: Page_274]

F I G U R E 2 Transposable element structures. Transposable elements can be classified into types I and II according to RNA intermediate production and insertion mechanisms. Type I, called retrotransposon, use RNA intermediate via a reverse transcription step, and can be divided into two groups. Long terminal repeats (LTR) elements with direct repeats both at beginning and at end of the element. It presents POL and GAG sequences related to retroviral protein genes. Non-LTR elements also use an RNA intermediate and are characterized by a polyA tail. Short interspersed nuclear elements (SINEs) are non-autonomous transposable element (TE) that will use LINE enzymatic machinery to transpose. Type II elements, named DNA transposons, present terminal inverted repeats (TIR) at each extremity, which are recognized by transposon's transposase and allow the integration in other genome. Miniature inverted repeat transposable elements (MITEs) have no open reading frames (ORFs) and are non-autonomous TEs. Then, helitron transposons use DNA helicase mechanisms to be transposed and do not present TIR pattern. Hence, the recently discovered Maverick subgroup seems to use a self-encoded DNA polymerase and have TIRs [SOURCE: Page_276]

### 1. Présentation synthétique de la publication Genitoni et al. en révision

La capacité des plantes invasives à coloniser rapidement de nouveaux milieux pose la question de leurs [SOURCE: Page_290]

sources de flexibilité. Rey et al. (2016) ainsi que Marin/Genitoni et al. (2019) présentent les éléments [SOURCE: Page_290]

transposables et les mécanismes épigénétiques comme une source de flexibilité qui pourrait participer à [SOURCE: Page_290]

cette. La méthylation de l’ADN intervient dans nombreux processus du développement des plantes, mais [SOURCE: Page_290]

également dans la réponse à l’environnement. Pourtant, il existe encore peu d’études sur les modèles [SOURCE: Page_290]

invasifs. [SOURCE: Page_290]

L’objectif de ce travail est d’étudier la méthylation de l’ADN chez une plante invasive dans la [SOURCE: Page_290]

réponse au changement de milieu. Ludwigia grandiflora, est une plante invasive aquatique pour laquelle [SOURCE: Page_290]

un morphotype terrestre a récemment été décrit. Cette invasion secondaire fait de cette espèce un bon [SOURCE: Page_290]

candidat pour l’étude des mécanismes d’adaptation rapide. (Haury et al., 2014; Billet et al., 2018). Nous [SOURCE: Page_290]

faisons l’hypothèse que les morphotypes terrestre et aquatique de la jussie en réponse au changement de [SOURCE: Page_290]

milieu (terrestre ou aquatique) présentent des différences dans leur pourcentage de méthylation. [SOURCE: Page_290]

Pour tester cette hypothèse, nous avons adopté une approche corrélative basée sur l’utilisation [SOURCE: Page_290]

d’un agent pharmacologique hypométhylant, appelé zébularine. L’effet de ce traitement qui doit [SOURCE: Page_290]

diminuer artificiellement le niveau de méthylation de l’ADN a été ensuite analysé. Ainsi, nous avons [SOURCE: Page_290]

sur les tissus néo-formés (feuilles et racines) (1) évalué le pourcentage de méthylation global (par HPLC) [SOURCE: Page_290]

des morphotypes en condition aquatique et terrestre, puis nous avons (2) quantifié les impacts de [SOURCE: Page_290]

l’hypométhylation sur des traits physiologiques (morphologie et développement, métabolites et [SOURCE: Page_290]

phytohormones). Nous avons observé que si le niveau de méthylation global est identique entre les [SOURCE: Page_290]

256 [SOURCE: Page_291]

257 [SOURCE: Page_292]

morphotypes et conditions sans traitement hypométhylant, la zébularine a bien induit une [SOURCE: Page_292]

hypométhylation comme attendu dans les parties néoformées au cours du traitement chez les deux [SOURCE: Page_292]

morphotypes, et ce indépendamment des conditions. Cette hypométhylation est associée à des [SOURCE: Page_292]

changements physiologiques. Une analyse intégrative de type ACP de toutes ces variables indique que [SOURCE: Page_292]

le morphotype aquatique hypométhylé tendrait à se rapprocher des caractéristiques du morphotype [SOURCE: Page_292]

terrestre témoin. [SOURCE: Page_292]

Nos résultats suggèrent une possible implication de la méthylation de l’ADN et des [SOURCE: Page_292]

phytohormones dans la colonisation du milieu terrestre par la jussie et encouragent notamment à [SOURCE: Page_292]

appliquer une stratégie épigénomique sur ce modèle (voir « perspectives » dans la partie 4). [SOURCE: Page_292]

Cet article a fait l’objet d’une première révision dans la revue Physiologia plantarum. Les [SOURCE: Page_292]

reviewers ont notamment abordé trois points clés pour améliorer ce papier : [SOURCE: Page_292]

- Le premier point, le plus important, stipulait l’absence de données génétiques concernant la [SOURCE: Page_292]

diversité entre les deux morphotypes de Ludwigia grandiflora. Ce manque rendait nos conclusions trop [SOURCE: Page_292]

spéculatives quant au rôle de l’épigénétique. Les résultats de diversité génétique sont une composante [SOURCE: Page_292]

de la thèse de Luis Portillo (2017-2020). Ainsi des données génétiques sur la diversité des morphotypes [SOURCE: Page_292]

aquatique et terrestre ont été obtenues. Ainsi, il existe une diversité génétique importante au sein de la [SOURCE: Page_292]

population du marais de Mazerolles, mais il n’y a pas de structuration significative au sein de cette [SOURCE: Page_292]

population. Ces résultats vont être intégrés à l’article et nous reverrons nos conclusions pour y ajouter [SOURCE: Page_292]

la composante génétique. [SOURCE: Page_292]

- Le second point concernait le manque de quantification de la plasticité phénotypique pourtant [SOURCE: Page_292]

abordé dans l’article. Nous proposons de calculer l’indice de plasticité RDPI et d’ajouter un tableau [SOURCE: Page_292]

statistique de ces analyses en données supplémentaires. [SOURCE: Page_292]

- Enfin, les reviewers ont questionné les analyses statistiques utilisées et l’absence de certains [SOURCE: Page_292]

résultats statistiques dans les tableaux et les figures. Les tableaux et figures ont été corrigés dans ce sens. [SOURCE: Page_292]

Avec l’aide d’un statisticien, nous allons retravailler voire faire évoluer le choix des tests utilisés. [SOURCE: Page_292]

La publication est ainsi en révision et sera resoumise prochainement après avoir inclus la [SOURCE: Page_292]

réponse aux demandes justifiés des reviewers. [SOURCE: Page_292]

### 2. Publication Genitoni et al. en révision (Physiologia plantarum)

Hypomethylation of the aquatic invasive plant, Ludwigia grandiflora, mimics the [SOURCE: Page_294]

adaptive transition into terrestrial morphotype [SOURCE: Page_294]

Julien Genitoni^1,2, Danièle Vassaux^1, Alain Delaunay^2, Sylvie Citerne^3, David Renault^4, Dominique [SOURCE: Page_294]

Barloy^1*, Stéphane Maury^2 1 ESE, Ecology and Ecosystem Health, Agrocampus Ouest, INRA, Rennes, France 2 Laboratoire de Biologie des Ligneux et des Grandes Cultures (LBLGC), EA1207 USC1328 INRA, [SOURCE: Page_294]

Université d’Orléans, 45067, Orléans, France 3 Plateau Technique de Chimie du Végétal, Institut Jean-Pierre Bourgin, Versailles, France 4 UMR CNRS 6553 EcoBio, University of Rennes 1, Rennes, France [SOURCE: Page_294]

   Corresponding author: [EMAIL_REDACTED] [SOURCE: Page_294]

Abstract [SOURCE: Page_294]

Ongoing global changes affect ecosystems and open up new opportunities for biological invasion. The [SOURCE: Page_294]

ability of invasive species to rapidly adapt to new environments represents a relevant model to study [SOURCE: Page_294]

short-term adapting mechanisms. The aquatic invasive plant, Ludwigia grandiflora, is classified as [SOURCE: Page_294]

harmful in rivers in Europe. Its recent dispersion in wet meadows, especially in France, has led to the [SOURCE: Page_294]

appearence of two distinct morphotypes. Indeed, L. grandiflora showed rapid transition from aquatic to [SOURCE: Page_294]

terrestrial morphotypes in less than five years. Here, we investigate epigenetic as a possible source of [SOURCE: Page_294]

flexibility involved in this fast terrestrial transition. To test this hypothesis, artifitial hypomethylation [SOURCE: Page_294]

was induced on both morphotypes. Both morphotype responses were evaluated by analysing global [SOURCE: Page_294]

DNA methylation, morphological changes, phytohormones and metabolites profiles in both aquatic and [SOURCE: Page_294]

terrestrial conditions in shoot and root tissues. Hypomethylation significantly affected morphological [SOURCE: Page_294]

260 [SOURCE: Page_295]

261 [SOURCE: Page_296]

variables such as leaf numbers and biomass production, phytohormones levels such as auxin and [SOURCE: Page_296]

salicylic acid and some metabolite amounts, as sugars and amino acids. Our results showed that effects [SOURCE: Page_296]

of hypomethylation depend on morphotypes, conditions and plant tissues highlighting differences [SOURCE: Page_296]

among the morphotypes and their plasticity. Finally, using a correlative integrative approach, the [SOURCE: Page_296]

hypomethylation of the aquatic morphotype was shown to mimic the characteristics of the terrestrial [SOURCE: Page_296]

morphotype. Altogether, our data suggest that DNA methylation may play a key role in Ludwigia [SOURCE: Page_296]

grandiflora plasticity during its terrestrial fast transition. [SOURCE: Page_296]

Keywords: Water primrose, Epigenetics, DNA methylation, Metabolite, Phytohormone. [SOURCE: Page_296]

Introduction [SOURCE: Page_298]

Global change and human activity impact ecosystems and allow new opportunities for geographic [SOURCE: Page_298]

expansion of invasive species (van Kleunen et al. 2015, Early et al. 2016). Yet, the capability of the [SOURCE: Page_298]

organisms to adapt rapidly to the newly encountered environmental conditions is crucial for the [SOURCE: Page_298]

establishement of a viable population. This is especially true for plant species that are constrained to [SOURCE: Page_298]

immobility. Moreover, invasion processes can occasionally result in bottlenecks, i.e. a large decrease of [SOURCE: Page_298]

the genetic diversity of the few surviving propagules. In spite of this situation, they spread and cause [SOURCE: Page_298]

economic and ecological issues (Theoharides and Dukes 2007). Rapid adaptive mechanisms such as [SOURCE: Page_298]

phenotypic plasticity, which is the ability of one genotype to produce several phenotypes according to [SOURCE: Page_298]

the environment (Pigliucci 2005), are commonly cited as an important factor favouring the invasion [SOURCE: Page_298]

success. Theoretically, organisms characterized by a greater plasticity should be able to thrive in a larger [SOURCE: Page_298]

range of environmental conditions, as compared with their less plastic relatives. While high level of [SOURCE: Page_298]

phenotypic plasticity reported in invasive species, (Trussell and Smith 2000, Sexton et al. 2002, Daehler [SOURCE: Page_298]

2003, Davidson et al. 2011, Morris 2014) is still under debate (Chown et al. 2007, Godoy et al. 2011, [SOURCE: Page_298]

Matzek, 2012, Lamarque et al. 2013), the sources of flexibility in invasive species remains to be [SOURCE: Page_298]

established. [SOURCE: Page_298]

Epigenetics can be defined as any non‐genetic molecular modification of the genome that alters [SOURCE: Page_298]

gene expression (Meyer, 2018). This definition broadly encompasses several levels of chromatin [SOURCE: Page_298]

modifications, including DNA methylation, histone modifications and variants, non-coding RNAs [SOURCE: Page_298]

(Duncan et al. 2014, Allis and Jenuwein 2016). Epigenetics has been recently proposed as a potential [SOURCE: Page_298]

source of flexibility involved in the success of invasive species by allowing organisms to express [SOURCE: Page_298]

advantageous phenotypes across a broader range of environments (Richards 2006, Richards et al. 2017, [SOURCE: Page_298]

for a recent review see Marin et al. 2019). Indeed, these last years many studies have highlighted the [SOURCE: Page_298]

role of epigenetics in many mechanisms in plants, such as development (Guo et al. 2018, Li et al. 2018), [SOURCE: Page_298]

responses to biotic and abiotic stress, (Tricker 2015, Crisp et al. 2016, Lämke and Bäurle, 2017), [SOURCE: Page_298]

memory and priming (Mauch-Mani et al. 2017, Le Gac et al. 2018, Sow et al. 2018, Le Gac et al. 2019), [SOURCE: Page_298]

phenotypic plasticity (Gourcilleau et al. 2010, Becker et al. 2011, Schmitz et al. 2011, Baulcombe and [SOURCE: Page_298]

Dean 2014, Kooke et al. 2015, Conde et al. 2017, Lafon-Placette et al. 2018, Maury et al. 2019) and [SOURCE: Page_298]

264 [SOURCE: Page_299]

265 [SOURCE: Page_300]

possibly adaptation (Bräutigam et al. 2013, Kawakatsu et al. 2016, Rey et al. 2016, Schmid et [SOURCE: Page_300]

al. 2018, Gourcilleau et al. 2019). Thus, Kooke et al. (2015), using epiRILs on Arabidopsis thaliana [SOURCE: Page_300]

based on ddm 1-2 lines, tested morphological responses after salin condition. They found several [SOURCE: Page_300]

phenotypes among epiRILs and that hypomethylation affects phenotypic plasticity in stress response. [SOURCE: Page_300]

While the role of epigenetics and transposable elements in invasive processes could be key sources of [SOURCE: Page_300]

flexibility for invasive species during colonisation of new environment, actual available studies have [SOURCE: Page_300]

only established correlations between methylation patterns, phenotypes and environments (Gao et al. [SOURCE: Page_300]

2010, Richards et al. 2012, Xie et al. 2015, Marin et al. 2019). [SOURCE: Page_300]

Epigenomics methods such as Whole-Genome Bisulfite Sequencing (WGBS) can provide [SOURCE: Page_300]

detailed information at the scale of the cytosines over the whole genome (Yong et al. 2016), these [SOURCE: Page_300]

approaches require a complete reference genome. Other methods using pharmacological approach with [SOURCE: Page_300]

a hypomethylating agent as zebularine and 5-azacytidine are commonly used. Such a strategy has [SOURCE: Page_300]

already been reported successfully in model plants such as Arabidopsis thaliana (Baubec et al. 2009, [SOURCE: Page_300]

Amoah et al. 2012) and many others (Burn et al. 1993, Brock and Davidson 1994, Finnegan et al. 1998, [SOURCE: Page_300]

Fieldes et al. 2005, Causevic et al. 2006, Trap-Gentil et al. 2011) but not in invasive plants. The global [SOURCE: Page_300]

DNA methylation (%mC), is a widely used and proven epigenetic indicator in plants (Causevic et al. [SOURCE: Page_300]

2006, Gourcilleau et al. 2010, Trap-Gentil et al. 2011, Teyssier et al. 2014, Alonso et al. 2015, Alonso [SOURCE: Page_300]

et al. 2016, Le Gac et al. 2018, Sow et al. 2018, Gourcilleau et al. 2019) using the most approved HPLC [SOURCE: Page_300]

technique (Lambé et al. 1997, Trap-Gentil et al. 2011, Teyssier et al. 2014, Alonso et al. 2016, [SOURCE: Page_300]

Kurdyukov and Bullock 2016, Yong et al. 2016, Sow et al. 2018). [SOURCE: Page_300]

Ludwigia grandiflora, subsp. hexapetala, native to South America, is an aquatic invasive plant [SOURCE: Page_300]

in Europe (Hussner et al. 2016). L. grandiflora can live in a wide range of environments (Haury et al. [SOURCE: Page_300]

2014). In France, it colonizes aquatic habitats, such as static or slow-flowing waters, river banks and [SOURCE: Page_300]

more recently wet meadows (Dandelot et al. 2005, Lambert et al. 2010). As mentioned in Billet et al. [SOURCE: Page_300]

(2018), L. grandiflora is an amphibious plant characterized by an aquatic morphotype (Am). Recently, [SOURCE: Page_300]

water primrose invaded wet meadows and a new terrestrial morphotype (Tm) appeared. The population [SOURCE: Page_300]

266 [SOURCE: Page_301]

267 [SOURCE: Page_302]

studied in Billet et al. (2018) appeared in France in 1995 for the aquatic morphotype and five years later [SOURCE: Page_302]

for the terrestrial one. This secondary invasion could lead to loss of financial support for farmers because [SOURCE: Page_302]

of depreciation of fodder value and abandonment of pasturing. This begs the question of fast adaptation [SOURCE: Page_302]

of this invasive plant to a new environment. Am in its original condition is characterized by an elongated [SOURCE: Page_302]

morphology with few leaf number, on the contrary Tm presents a bushy morphology with a greater root [SOURCE: Page_302]

system and more leaves than aquatic morphotype (Haury et al. 2014, Billet et al. 2018). [SOURCE: Page_302]

Water primrose reproduces essentially by clonal propagation, one population should exhibit low [SOURCE: Page_302]

genetic diversity and makes it a good candidate to test the role of epigenetic mechanisms in invasive [SOURCE: Page_302]

plants according to Zhang et al. (2013). The aim of this study is to explore the involvement of an [SOURCE: Page_302]

epigenetic component in the adaptation of L. grandiflora to the terrestrial environment. We hypothesized [SOURCE: Page_302]

that DNA methylation is differently mobilized by terrestrial and aquatic morphotypes according to [SOURCE: Page_302]

environment and involved in the fast terrestrial transition, as it was suggested in changing environment [SOURCE: Page_302]

for A.thaliana and Alternanthera philoxeroides (Li et al. 2013). Here, we used a pharmacological [SOURCE: Page_302]

approach using zebularine to perturbate DNA methylation on Am and Tm from the same population of [SOURCE: Page_302]

L. grandiflora previously studied in Billet et al. (2018) in response to aquatic and terrestrial conditions. [SOURCE: Page_302]

To characterize the hypomethylation effect of zebularine, a correlative approach was conducted using [SOURCE: Page_302]

morphological, physiological (metabolomics and phytohormones) and methylation percentage [SOURCE: Page_302]

variables. [SOURCE: Page_302]

Material and methods [SOURCE: Page_302]

Plant material and experimental design [SOURCE: Page_302]

Aquatic (Am) and terrestrial (Tm) morphotypes of L. grandiflora were collected from the Mazerolles [SOURCE: Page_302]

swamps (Nantes, France, N47 23.260, W$_1$ 28.206). After collection, plants were grown in a greenhouse [SOURCE: Page_302]

in aquatic condition for Am and in terrestrial conditions for Tm (Billet et al. 2018). [SOURCE: Page_302]

For the zebularine experiment, a 10 cm portion from the stem apex was collected, without roots, [SOURCE: Page_302]

buds, and lateral stems. All plants were preconditioned during 2 weeks, as described in Billet et al. [SOURCE: Page_302]

(2018) to promote root development. For morphological analyses, two replicates of nine plants were [SOURCE: Page_302]

268 [SOURCE: Page_303]

269 [SOURCE: Page_304]

randomly grouped by three plants per container for aquatic (Am-a and Tm-a) and terrestrial [SOURCE: Page_304]

(Am-t and Tm-t) conditions for both morphotypes. The plants were then placed in a growth chamber [SOURCE: Page_304]

(22°C, 16 h day/8 h night). Similarly, three replicates of six plants were carried out for physiological [SOURCE: Page_304]

(phytohormones and metabolites quantifications) and %mC analyses for each morphotype (Am and [SOURCE: Page_304]

Tm), condition (-a and -t) and treatment (ctrl and zeb) combination, for a total of 288 plants. Zebularine [SOURCE: Page_304]

(Sigma-Aldrich) treatment at 150 µM was applied in the liquid solution at the beginning of the [SOURCE: Page_304]

experiment and renewed 7 days later. Plants without zebularine were grown as a control. Morphology [SOURCE: Page_304]

sampling for physiological and methylation analyses were conducted 14 days after the beginning of the [SOURCE: Page_304]

experiment. De novo shoots and roots, taken five centimeters from the apex (including stems, leaves, [SOURCE: Page_304]

and buds) were sampled separately from six randomly collected plants per morphotype (Am or Tm), [SOURCE: Page_304]

treatment (zebularine or control) and condition (aquatic or terrestrial). Samples for physiological [SOURCE: Page_304]

analysis were pooled and immediately snap-frozen in liquid nitrogen, then lyophilized over 48 hr using [SOURCE: Page_304]

a Cosmos 20K (Cryotec, Saint-Gély-du-Fesc, France) and stored at −80°C. [SOURCE: Page_304]

Morphological analyses [SOURCE: Page_304]

Nine plants per morphotype, condition and treatment were analysed. The following morphological, [SOURCE: Page_304]

growth and fitness traits were measured: [SOURCE: Page_304]

Length of the plant (LP) in centimeter (cm), number of internodes (nbI), and number of leaves [SOURCE: Page_304]

(nbL), which characterize plant morphology. The length of internodes in centimeter was calculated as [SOURCE: Page_304]

the ratio of LP/nbI. Number of nodes with roots (nbNR), number of nodes with buds (nbB) variables are [SOURCE: Page_304]

associated with the fitness of the plant. As mentioned in Billet et al., 2018, fitness of L. grandiflora is [SOURCE: Page_304]

considered as the ability to produce propagules from buds or nodes with roots. L. grandiflora has the [SOURCE: Page_304]

ability to form new plant from small (>1 cm) plant fragments. Biomass of plants in grams (g) was [SOURCE: Page_304]

determined by measuring the fresh mass of shoots (FMS) and roots (FMR). After oven drying the [SOURCE: Page_304]

samples at 105°C for 48 h, we obtained their respective dry mass (DMS and DMR). To determine water [SOURCE: Page_304]

content, the ratios of fresh/dry mass of shoots (Sr) and roots (Rr) were calculated. [SOURCE: Page_304]

271 [SOURCE: Page_306]

DNA extraction and determination of global DNA methylation percentage by HPLC [SOURCE: Page_306]

Genomic DNA extraction was carried out using the CTAB protocol described in Lafon-Placette et al., [SOURCE: Page_306]

(2013). Quantity and quality of gDNA were checked by NanoDrop spectrometer and electrophoresis on [SOURCE: Page_306]

agarose gel and ethidium bromide staining under UV light. Genomic DNA was hydrolyzed into [SOURCE: Page_306]

nucleosides and analyzed by HPLC using a GeminiTM column (150 × 4.6 mm, 5 µm; Phenomenex, Le [SOURCE: Page_306]

Pecq, France). Finally, an isocratic mobile phase consisting of 0.5% methanol (v/v) and 5 mM acetic [SOURCE: Page_306]

acid in water, as described by Zhu et al. (2013) and Le Gac et al. (2018) was used. Global DNA [SOURCE: Page_306]

methylcytosine percentage (% mC) was calculated as follows: [SOURCE: Page_306]

%mC=(mC/(C+mC))×100, [SOURCE: Page_306]

where C is the 2ʹ-deoxycytidine content and mC is the 5-methyl-2ʹ-deoxycytidine content. For each set [SOURCE: Page_306]

of conditions, we analyzed three biological replicates for each morphotype, condition and treatment. [SOURCE: Page_306]

Each sample was hydrolyzed twice and two HPLC runs were carried out by hydrolysis. Controls for this [SOURCE: Page_306]

procedure included the use of co-migration with commercial standards (Sigma-Aldrich), confirmation [SOURCE: Page_306]

by enzyme restriction analysis and tests for RNA contamination were based on the HPLC detection of [SOURCE: Page_306]

ribonucleosides which have already been detailed in Zhu et al. (2013). [SOURCE: Page_306]

Phytohormone quantification [SOURCE: Page_306]

Quantification of Abscisic acid (ABA), Salicylic acid (SA), Jasmonic acid (JA), Jasmonyl Leucine acid [SOURCE: Page_306]

(JLA) and Auxins (IAA) were carried out in both shoots and roots. For each sample, 1 mg of dry powder [SOURCE: Page_306]

was extracted with 0.8 mL of acetone/water/acetic acid (80/19/1 v:v:v). Phytohormones stable labelled [SOURCE: Page_306]

isotopes used as internal standards were prepared as described in (Roux et al. 2014). 1 ng of each [SOURCE: Page_306]

standard was added to the sample. The extract was vigorously shaken for 1min, sonicated for 1 min at [SOURCE: Page_306]

25 Hz, shaken for 10 minutes at 10°C in a Thermomixer (Eppendorf®, and then centrifuged (8,000g, 10 [SOURCE: Page_306]

°C, 10 min.). The supernatants were collected, and the pellets were re-extracted twice with 0.4 mL of [SOURCE: Page_306]

the same extraction solution, then vigorously shaken (1 min) and sonicated (1 min; 25 Hz). After the [SOURCE: Page_306]

centrifugations, the three supernatants were pooled and dried (Final Volume 1.6 mL). [SOURCE: Page_306]

273 [SOURCE: Page_308]

Each dry extract was dissolved in 100 µL of acetonitrile/water (50/50 v/v), filtered, and analyzed [SOURCE: Page_308]

using a Waters Acquity ultra performance liquid chromatograph coupled to a Waters Xevo Triple [SOURCE: Page_308]

quadrupole mass spectrometer TQS (UPLC-ESI-MS/MS). The compounds were separated on a reverse- [SOURCE: Page_308]

phase column (Uptisphere C18 UP3HDO, 100*2.1 mm*3µm particle size; Interchim, France) using a [SOURCE: Page_308]

flow rate of 0.4 mL min-1 and a binary gradient: (A) acetic acid 0.1 % in water (v/v) and (B) acetonitrile [SOURCE: Page_308]

with 0.1 % acetic acid, the column temperature was 40 °C, for Abscisic acid, salicylic acid, jasmonic [SOURCE: Page_308]

acid, and indole-3-acetic acid we used the following binary gradient (time, % A): (0 min., 98 %), (3 [SOURCE: Page_308]

min., 70 %), (7.5 min., 50 %), (8.5 min., 5 %), (9.6 min., 0%), (13.2 min., 98 %), (15.7 min., 98 %), [SOURCE: Page_308]

Mass spectrometry was conducted in electrospray and Multiple Reaction Monitoring scanning mode [SOURCE: Page_308]

(MRM mode), in positive ion mode for the indole-3-acetic acid and in negative ion mode for the other [SOURCE: Page_308]

hormones. Relevant instrumental parameters were set as follows: capillary 1.5 kV (negative mode), [SOURCE: Page_308]

source block and desolvation gas temperatures 130 °C and 500 °C, respectively. Nitrogen was used to [SOURCE: Page_308]

assist the cone and desolvation (150 L h-1 and 800 L h-1, respectively), argon was used as the collision [SOURCE: Page_308]

gas at a flow of 0.18 mL min-1. [SOURCE: Page_308]

Metabolomic fingerprint [SOURCE: Page_308]

Gas chromatography coupled with mass spectrometry (GC‐MS) was used to scan for the metabolites [SOURCE: Page_308]

that could be detected from the samples (amino acids, organic acids, polyamines, polyols, or sugars). [SOURCE: Page_308]

For the preparation of the samples, the method described in Serra et al. (2013) was used and adapted as [SOURCE: Page_308]

in Billet et al. (2018). Briefly, for each sample, an aliquot of 10 mg of lyophilized powder was [SOURCE: Page_308]

homogenized in 600 μl of a solution of ice‐cold methanol/chloroform (2:1, v/v). Then, a volume of [SOURCE: Page_308]

400 μl of ultra‐pure water was added. Samples were homogenized and centrifuged for 10 min at 4,000 g [SOURCE: Page_308]

(4°C). One hundred and twenty and eighty microliters of the upper phase containing metabolites were [SOURCE: Page_308]

transferred to new glass vials for roots and shoots respectively. The derivatization of the samples was [SOURCE: Page_308]

conducted with a CTC CombiPAL autosampler (CTC Analytics AG, Zwingen, Switzerland), as [SOURCE: Page_308]

described in Serra et al. (2013). The GC-MS platform consisted in an Agilent 7890B gas chromatograph [SOURCE: Page_308]

274 [SOURCE: Page_309]

275 [SOURCE: Page_310]

coupled to a 5977B mass spectrometer. The injector was held at 250°C, and the temperature of the oven [SOURCE: Page_310]

ranged from 70 to 170 °C at 5 °C per mon, fom 170 to 280 °C at 7 °C per min, and from 280 to 320 °C [SOURCE: Page_310]

at 15 °C per min; at the end of the temperature ramps, the oven remained at 320 °C for 4 min. A 30 m [SOURCE: Page_310]

fused silica column (HP$_5$ MS 30 m, I.D. 0.25 mm, thickness 0.25 µm, 5% Diphenyl / 95% [SOURCE: Page_310]

Dimethylpolysiloxan, Agilent Technologies) was used, with helium as the gas carrier at 1 mL per min. [SOURCE: Page_310]

The temperatures of the transfer line and ion source were 280 and 230 °C, respectively. The split mode [SOURCE: Page_310]

(split ratio: 2:1) was used for the injection of 1 µL of each sample, and detection was realized by [SOURCE: Page_310]

electronic impact (electron energy: 70 eV), in full scan mode. The detected peaks were annotated with [SOURCE: Page_310]

MassHunter. Most detected metabolites were identified, and calibration curves were drawn for [SOURCE: Page_310]

calculating concentration of each metabolite. [SOURCE: Page_310]

Statistical analysis [SOURCE: Page_310]

The effect of the zebularine treatment on the morphology and physiology of both morphotypes was [SOURCE: Page_310]

assessed by running principal component analyses (PCAs) and analyses of variance (ANOVAs). Four- [SOURCE: Page_310]

way ANOVA were carried out with morphotype, treatment, condition and biological replicate as factors [SOURCE: Page_310]

and three-way ANOVA without using morphotype as a factor. Then two and three way interactions were [SOURCE: Page_310]

analyzed. The residuals normality and the homoscedasticity were verified by Shapiro–Wilk's and [SOURCE: Page_310]

Bartlett's tests, and normality was achieved, when required by transforming morphological traits and the [SOURCE: Page_310]

metabolite concentrations (Log^10). The Tukey’s test was used to compare means for all data. [SOURCE: Page_310]

Finally, we tried to link metabolites where concentration varied among the experimental [SOURCE: Page_310]

treatments with metabolic pathways. To achieve this goal, we performed pathway enrichment analyses [SOURCE: Page_310]

in Metaboanalyst 3.0 (Xia et al. 2015). Fisher's exact test algorithm was performed for these pathway [SOURCE: Page_310]

analyses, with Arabidopsis thaliana as the reference model. In this procedure, the number of hits [SOURCE: Page_310]

between the metabolites in our dataset and all metabolites of a given pathway was calculated. Data [SOURCE: Page_310]

presented in the figures are untransformed. [SOURCE: Page_310]

Results [SOURCE: Page_312]

Zebularine induces hypomethylation in the aquatic and terrestrial morphotypes of the invasive L. [SOURCE: Page_312]

grandiflora plant. [SOURCE: Page_312]

A 14-day zebularine treatment was applied to induce DNA hypomethylation on Am and Tm of the [SOURCE: Page_312]

invasive L. grandiflora plant grown in aquatic and terrestrial conditions. Only de novo formed shoots [SOURCE: Page_312]

during the treatment were used to assess the global DNA methylation percentage (%mC) by HPLC [SOURCE: Page_312]

method (Fig. 1; see Materials and Methods for procedure). The methylation percentages ranged from [SOURCE: Page_312]

25.9% to 29.8% for control plants and from 20.9% to 23.9% for plant treated with zebularine (Fig. 1). [SOURCE: Page_312]

A 4-way analysis of variance was carried out by comparison of morphotype (Am or Tm), treatment [SOURCE: Page_312]

(zebularine or control), condition (aquatic or terrestrial) and biological replicate. DNA methylation [SOURCE: Page_312]

percentage was significantly effected by morphotypes, treatment and the interaction between condition [SOURCE: Page_312]

and treatment (p = 8.82e-03, 4.88e-08 and 1.86e-2, respectively). Anova analysis revealed a significant [SOURCE: Page_312]

decrease of %mC in zebularine-treated plants (p = 4.88e-08). Specifically, the zebularine treatment [SOURCE: Page_312]

induced a methylation decrease ranging from 7.2% and 8.6% for Am and Tm grown in terrestrial [SOURCE: Page_312]

condition and from 4.3% and 5.1 % in aquatic condition, respectively (Fig. 1). However, we observed [SOURCE: Page_312]

similar methylation levels between morphotypes independently of conditions for both treatments. [SOURCE: Page_312]

The data showed that no significant variation of global DNA methylation was observed among [SOURCE: Page_312]

morphotypes and conditions but a significant hypomethylation was obtained after a 14 days zebularine [SOURCE: Page_312]

treatment in both morphotypes and conditions. [SOURCE: Page_312]

Hypomethylation of both morphotypes affects growth and morphology in aquatic and terrestrial [SOURCE: Page_312]

conditions. [SOURCE: Page_312]

After a 14-day treatment, Am and Tm grown in aquatic (-a) and terrestrial (-t) conditions were pictured [SOURCE: Page_312]

(Fig. 2a) and analysed for morphology, biomass and water content traits (Fig. 2b). While no necrosis [SOURCE: Page_312]

symptom was observed for zebularine-treated plants (Fig. 2a), morphology and growth of the plants [SOURCE: Page_312]

appeared to be affected, for example with an increased number of leaves in hypomethylated Am in [SOURCE: Page_312]

aquatic condition (Fig. 2a). Analyses of variance were carried out (morphotype, condition, treatment, [SOURCE: Page_312]

biological replicate, double or triple interactions; Fig. 2b, Table S$_1$ and see supplementary traits [SOURCE: Page_312]

The main observation was that the hypomethylated aquatic morphotype in aquatic and terrestrial [SOURCE: Page_320]

conditions (Am-a-zeb and Am-t-zeb; Fig. 5a) were getting closer on the PCA to the control terrestrial [SOURCE: Page_320]

morphotype in each condition (Tm-a-ctrl and Tm-t-ctrl, respectively). [SOURCE: Page_320]

Another PCA with metabolomic data was tested using a subset of metabolites not to unbalance [SOURCE: Page_320]

the analysis. Six metabolites showing significant correlations with %mC (Fig.S$_4$) and other metabolites [SOURCE: Page_320]

significantly affected by hypomethylation according to anova and t-test were selected (Fig.S$_5$). The [SOURCE: Page_320]

effect of hypomethylation was mainly observed this time in the aquatic condition explained principally [SOURCE: Page_320]

by Water Content (WC), shoot ratio (Sr) and some metabolites in shoots, such as organic acid [SOURCE: Page_320]

(phosphoric acid, aspartic acid), amino acid (phenylalanine, serine, leucine) and G3P (Fig. 5b). These [SOURCE: Page_320]

variables were significantly affected by zebularine on aquatic morphotype in aquatic condition (p<0.05 [SOURCE: Page_320]

and Fig.S$_1$). Based on mean comparison using tuckey-test, no significant difference was observed after [SOURCE: Page_320]

zebularine treatment between Tm-a-ctrl and Am-a-zeb, while significant difference between Tm-a-ctrl [SOURCE: Page_320]

and Am-a-ctrl remained (p<0.05 for WC, p<0.0001 for Sr). The other important result was [SOURCE: Page_320]

hypomethylated terrestrial morphotype, which showed different phenotype after hypomethylation. [SOURCE: Page_320]

Futhermore, according to metabolomic analysis terrestrial morphotype in aquatic condition has the most [SOURCE: Page_320]

diverse phenotype (Fig.S$_5$). [SOURCE: Page_320]

According to these integrative approaches, hypomethylation of the aquatic morphotype induces [SOURCE: Page_320]

a terrestrial morphotype-‘like’ situation, suggesting a role for epigenetics in the fast adaptation of the [SOURCE: Page_320]

aquatic invasive L.grandiflora to the terrestrial condition. [SOURCE: Page_320]

Discussion [SOURCE: Page_320]

Morphotypes of the invasive L. grandiflora plant showed distinct morphological and physiological [SOURCE: Page_320]

responses to aquatic and terrestrial conditions but similar global DNA methylation levels. [SOURCE: Page_320]

Ludwigia grandiflora originating from South America is an aquatic invasive plant in Europe (Hussner [SOURCE: Page_320]

et al. 2016) that has been reported in a wide range of environments (Haury et al. 2014) colonizing aquatic [SOURCE: Page_320]

habitats but also recently terrestrial ones with wet meadows becoming problematic for farmers [SOURCE: Page_320]

(Dandelot et al. 2005, Lambert et al. 2010). Two distinct invasive morphotypes, an aquatic and a [SOURCE: Page_320]

terrestrial one, have been identified (Haury et al. 2014, Billet et al. 2018). The present analysis confirms [SOURCE: Page_320]

these differences at the morphological and metabolomic levels (Billet et al. 2018). For example, as [SOURCE: Page_320]

286 [SOURCE: Page_321]

287 [SOURCE: Page_322]

shown by Billet et al. (2018) in their original conditions, aquatic morphotype has a lower number of [SOURCE: Page_322]

nodes with an elongated morphology, smaller number of leaves and stronger water content than [SOURCE: Page_322]

terrestrial morphotype. On the contrary, greater number of leaves and mass of roots significantly [SOURCE: Page_322]

characterized terrestrial morphotype. In addition, Billet et al. (2018) have identified a specific metabolite [SOURCE: Page_322]

accumulation in roots in terrestrial condition involving the three following pathways: amino sugar and [SOURCE: Page_322]

nucleotide sugar metabolism, the starch and sucrose metabolism and galactose, fructose, mannose [SOURCE: Page_322]

metabolism ; and two pathways in shoots in aquatic condition, the valine, leucine, and isoleucine [SOURCE: Page_322]

metabolism and degradation pathway. Here, if no significant differences using metaboanalyst were [SOURCE: Page_322]

detected, higher quantities of sugars in terrestrial condition and amino acids in aquatic condition were [SOURCE: Page_322]

found as described in Billet et al. (2018). [SOURCE: Page_322]

In the present work, we complete the initial characterization of these two morphotypes with the [SOURCE: Page_322]

quantification of phytohormones and DNA methylation levels. These two processes are well-known [SOURCE: Page_322]

regulators of plant development and their response to environmental variations (Sahu et al. 2013, Fang [SOURCE: Page_322]

et al. 2016, Li et al. 2018, Avramova 2019). Recently, it has also been proposed that phytohormone and [SOURCE: Page_322]

epigenetic act in crosstalk to ensure phenotypic plasticity (Yamamuro et al. 2016, Maury et al. 2019). [SOURCE: Page_322]

In our study, phytohormones were mainly observed to vary between conditions (plasticity) than between [SOURCE: Page_322]

morphotypes. Thus, ABA, JA and SA were present in greater amounts in terrestrial condition according [SOURCE: Page_322]

to their role in drought responses (Kohli et al. 2013). [SOURCE: Page_322]

Here, we analyzed two morphotypes originating from one clonally propagated population [SOURCE: Page_322]

thereby excluding or extremely reducing the effect of genetic variation and allowing to test the role of [SOURCE: Page_322]

epigenetic mechanisms in invasive plants (Zhang et al. 2013). In plants, DNA methylation is involved [SOURCE: Page_322]

in transposon silencing and gene expression that can change phenotype in response to environmental [SOURCE: Page_322]

variations (Lande 2009, Meyer 2015, Kawakatsu et al. 2016, Bewick and Schmitz 2017, Seymour and [SOURCE: Page_322]

Becker 2017). Although epigenomic methods such as whole-genome bisulfite sequencing (WGBS) [SOURCE: Page_322]

provide detailed information at the genomic scale, they require a complete reference genome that is still [SOURCE: Page_322]

lacking in L. grandiflora. In addition, this plant has been reported as a decaploid genome leading to a [SOURCE: Page_322]

complex situation (Dandelot et al. 2005). We measured the global DNA methylation (%mC) using the [SOURCE: Page_322]

most approved HPLC technique (Zhu et al. 2013, Kurdyukov and Bullock 2016). Although this [SOURCE: Page_322]

288 [SOURCE: Page_323]

289 [SOURCE: Page_324]

approach does not provide epigenetic characterization at the detailed level of genes and genomic regions. [SOURCE: Page_324]

It is a widely used and proven epigenetic indicator in plants accessible from the cell to the population [SOURCE: Page_324]

level (Lambé et al. 1997, Causevic et al. 2006, Gourcilleau et al. 2010, Raj et al. 2011, Trap-Gentil et [SOURCE: Page_324]

al. 2011, Latzel et al. 2013, Alonso et al. 2015, Garg et al. 2015, Alonso et al. 2016, Le Gac et al. 2018, [SOURCE: Page_324]

Sow et al. 2018, Gourcilleau et al. 2019, Le Gac et al. 2019). Here, we found that global methylation [SOURCE: Page_324]

level in L. grandiflora (estimated genome size around 700 Mb, personal communication D. Barloy) was [SOURCE: Page_324]

about ~28% of mC which is five times higher than in Arabidopsis thaliana (5%; 135Mb) and two times [SOURCE: Page_324]

higher than Antirrhinum majus (15%; 400-500Mb); consistent with the relation among global DNA [SOURCE: Page_324]

methylation (%mC) and the genome size reported in angiosperms (Alonso et al. 2015). However, in our [SOURCE: Page_324]

study, we could not detect any significant variation of %mC between morphotypes and conditions as [SOURCE: Page_324]

reported recently in isogenic lines of Antirrhinum majus in different shade avoidance conditions [SOURCE: Page_324]

(Gourcilleau et al. 2019). Few studies using MSAP technics are available (Marin et al. 2019) such as [SOURCE: Page_324]

one on the aquatic invasive species Alternanthera philoxeroides showing differences in DNA [SOURCE: Page_324]

methylation level according to aquatic and terrestrial forms, tissues, and flooding (Li et al. 2013). [SOURCE: Page_324]

Altogether, this proposes to further investigate methylation polymorphism in our system using [SOURCE: Page_324]

approaches that do not require a reference genome e.g., epigenome bisulfite sequencing (epiGBS), [SOURCE: Page_324]

bisulfite converted restriction site associated DNA sequencing (bsRADseq), Epi RADseq and [SOURCE: Page_324]

methylated DNA immunoprecipitation (meDIP)(van Gurp et al. 2016, Trucchi et al. 2016). However, [SOURCE: Page_324]

here our objective was an initial epigenetic characterization with a widely used epigenetic indicator [SOURCE: Page_324]

(%mC) and to assess the effect of zebularine treatment. [SOURCE: Page_324]

Zebularine induced hypomethylation on the L. grandiflora morphotypes in terrestrial and aquatic [SOURCE: Page_324]

conditions. [SOURCE: Page_324]

Hypomethylant chemical agents such as zebularine and 5-azacytidine are used in cancer research (Cheng [SOURCE: Page_324]

et al. 2004). In addition, there is a renewed use of the hypomethylant chemical agent for the study of [SOURCE: Page_324]

DNA methylation and its role in organism responses to the environment (Baubec et al. 2009, Bossdorf [SOURCE: Page_324]

et al. 2010, Richards et al. 2010, Hudson et al. 2011, Zhong et al. 2013, Latzel et al. 2016, Osorio- [SOURCE: Page_324]

Montalvo et al. 2018, Puy et al. 2018). Zebularine is an inhibitor of methyltransferase, which causes an [SOURCE: Page_324]

290 [SOURCE: Page_325]

291 [SOURCE: Page_326]

hypomethylation of de novo tissues. Our study was carried out at concentration and duration in [SOURCE: Page_326]

accordance to the cited literature. We assessed the %mC using HPLC method in de novo formed shoot [SOURCE: Page_326]

apex because it is the place where new tissues start their differentiated growth and development in [SOURCE: Page_326]

contact to zebularine (Aranda et al. 2017). We found that 14 days zebularine treatment induces a [SOURCE: Page_326]

significant decrease of %mC in de novo formed shoots for all situations (morphotypes x conditions) and [SOURCE: Page_326]

ranging from 4 and 9% as it was previously reported in Arabidopsis thaliana (Baubec et al. 2009). [SOURCE: Page_326]

Altogether, zebularine is an effective way to reduce the percentage of methylation in plant de [SOURCE: Page_326]

novo formed tissues. This allows us to generate, for the first time, hypomethylated L. grandiflora [SOURCE: Page_326]

morphotypes in both conditions to assess the impact of DNA hypomethylation on invasive plant’s fast [SOURCE: Page_326]

adaptation. [SOURCE: Page_326]

Induced hypomethylation affects morphotypes and their plasticity proposing a role of epigenetic [SOURCE: Page_326]

in the fast transition from aquatic to terrestrial morphotypes [SOURCE: Page_326]

Hypomethylated morphotypes in both terrestrial and aquatic conditions were shown to exhibit [SOURCE: Page_326]

significant variations compared to controls at the developmental, hormonal and metabolic levels. [SOURCE: Page_326]

Developmental effects induced by variations of DNA methylation have already been largely reported in [SOURCE: Page_326]

plants for example: Baubec et al. (2009) showed a reduction of growth after zebularine treatment in [SOURCE: Page_326]

Arabidopsis thaliana. Alonso et al. (2017) observed a decrease of leaf numbers after treatment with 5- [SOURCE: Page_326]

azacytidine and Tatra et al. (2000) reported stem elongation in Stellaria longipes in response to shade [SOURCE: Page_326]

using 5-azacytidine. Here, similar results were observed for Ludwigia grandiflora morphotypes but with [SOURCE: Page_326]

positive effect on development such as an increase of leaf and internode numbers. [SOURCE: Page_326]

Another main input of our analysis, was to combine developmental analysis with hormone and [SOURCE: Page_326]

metabolite levels. Phytohormones contribute not only to development but also to stress responses in [SOURCE: Page_326]

plants. In addition, there is growing evidence of a crosstalk between hormonal balance and epigenetic [SOURCE: Page_326]

regulation (Yamamuro et al. 2016, Zhang et al. 2016, Campos-Rivero et al. 2017, Maury et al. 2019). [SOURCE: Page_326]

Here, we showed that hormonal balances of SA, Auxine and LJA were affected in relation to [SOURCE: Page_326]

the plasticity of the morphotypes in changing conditions. In addition, we detected a significant negative [SOURCE: Page_326]

correlation between %mC and SA amount in roots. This is in accordance to Zhang et al. (2016) reporting [SOURCE: Page_326]

292 [SOURCE: Page_327]

293 [SOURCE: Page_328]

that the chromatin remodeler DDM$_1$, involved in DNA methylation patterns, promotes hybrid vigor by [SOURCE: Page_328]

regulating SA. In addition, connections between DNA methylation and hormone pathways in shoot apex [SOURCE: Page_328]

have been recently highlighted (Lafon-Placette et al. 2018, Le Gac et al. 2018, Maury et al. 2019). Few [SOURCE: Page_328]

studies suggested also relationships between phytohormones, metabolites and epigenetic mechanisms [SOURCE: Page_328]

(Latzel et al. 2012, Kooke et al. 2018, Schvartzman et al. 2018). Indeed, Kooke et al. (2018) found some [SOURCE: Page_328]

correlations between several EpiRIL of Arabidopsis thaliana and some secondary metabolites. Shen et [SOURCE: Page_328]

al. (2016) summarized interaction between metabolic/redox signaling with epigenetics according to [SOURCE: Page_328]

environmental conditions in plant adaptation suggesting a “bi-directional interplay” of epigenetics and [SOURCE: Page_328]

metabolism. Here, we found several metabolites (amino acids, sugars and organic acids) affected by [SOURCE: Page_328]

hypomethylation and six of them could be correlated to the %mC levels. However, the complex interplay [SOURCE: Page_328]

among epigenetic and metabolism needs more insight before being clearly interpreted. [SOURCE: Page_328]

Our fine characterization of the hypomethylation effects on the two invasive morphotypes in [SOURCE: Page_328]

terrestrial and aquatic conditions at the developmental, hormonal and metabolic levels allow us to carry [SOURCE: Page_328]

out an integrative approach using PCA. As we hypothesized, DNA hypomethylation impacted [SOURCE: Page_328]

differently aquatic and terrestrial morphotypes of L. grandiflora in response to both conditions. The [SOURCE: Page_328]

main outcome of this integrative analysis was that inducing hypomethylation on the aquatic morphotype [SOURCE: Page_328]

gives a control terrestrial morphotype like phenotype. Altogether, our data suggest that hypomethylation [SOURCE: Page_328]

of the invasive aquatic morphotype mimics the terrestrial fast transition and propose an implication of [SOURCE: Page_328]

the epigenome in the appearance of this new terrestrial invasive morphotype. Our data strongly supports [SOURCE: Page_328]

the actual hypothesis of a role of epigenetics in biological invasions (Marin et al. 2019) and the next [SOURCE: Page_328]

challenge will be to evaluate, at the genomic scale, the combined roles of epigenetics and transposable [SOURCE: Page_328]

elements. [SOURCE: Page_328]

### 3. Présentation synthétique de la publication Maury et al., 2019

L’interaction entre la dynamique de la chromatine et les phytohormones qui ressort de nos travaux est [SOURCE: Page_356]

un thème d’actualité. Nous avons particulièrement voulu travailler ce thème à travers une synthèse [SOURCE: Page_356]

bibliographique portant sur le méristème et de la plasticité phénotypique. Ce travail a ensuite été valorisé [SOURCE: Page_356]

sous la forme d’un article de revue (Maury et al., (2019) dans Frontiers in Plant Science). Cet article [SOURCE: Page_356]

replace succinctement le rôle des méristèmes dans le développement des plantes et présente les [SOURCE: Page_356]

mécanismes suggérant un lien étroit entre balance hormonale et mécanismes épigénétiques, avant [SOURCE: Page_356]

d’insister sur le rôle dans la plasticité. Enfin, nous avons proposé des perspectives pour l’étude de ces [SOURCE: Page_356]

interactions entre phytohormones et épigénétique. Celles-ci concernent l’amélioration des [SOURCE: Page_356]

méthodologies pour isoler et cultiver des cellules méristématiques à des stades de développement [SOURCE: Page_356]

particulier, la possibilité d’étendre ces études à des espèces d’intérêt agronomique en exploitant et [SOURCE: Page_356]

développant des nouvelles technologies, comme CRISPR-Cas^9, pour décrypter les liens entre [SOURCE: Page_356]

phytohormones et mécanismes épigénétiques. Bien que l’avancée des connaissances sur le modèle jussie [SOURCE: Page_356]

ne soit pas suffisante pour discuter d’une mécanistique aussi élaborée, ce travail donne des pistes [SOURCE: Page_356]

d’interprétation et des perspectives. [SOURCE: Page_356]

4. Publication : Maury et al 2019 (Frontiers in Plant Science) [SOURCE: Page_356]

Maury et al.                                                                                                                    Phytohormone and Chromatin Crosstalk [SOURCE: Page_359]

FIGURE 1 | Schematic model of phytohormones and chromatin crosstalk during plant developmental plasticity and robustness. Stem cell niches in SAM, RAM, or cambium are center of morphogenesis giving rise to the aerial and root systems or wood formation in perennials and plasticity in response to various environmental cues. Environmental signals are perceived directly or indirectly by meristems and could affect hormonal balance and/or chromatin structure in a complex crosstalk: (1) hormones can alter chromatin structure and modifiers or (2) chromatin can regulate hormones signaling/biosynthesis. These two mechanisms could then interact separately (3 and 4), jointly or successively (5) affecting genes expression and /or TEs mobilization. Thus, the hormone/chromatin crosstalk can participate in developmental choice (Robustness vs. Plasticity) by controlling cell gene identity in meristems, hormone balance integration, or chromatin stabilization of gene expression. While most of these changes are transient (resetting of hormonal and chromatin modifications) allowing the plant to be respond to new environmental conditions, chromatin states could be maintained through cell division allowing an epigenetic memory and a potential priming of new meristem-derived-organs.
